studies.title: Mercy Written Upon Himself
studies.meaning: A question is put and then answered by the same speaker, a form used when the answer is not actually in dispute. Everything belongs to God. What follows is the surprising part: the one who owns everything has bound Himself, and the verb chosen is the one for putting a contract in writing. Mercy is described as a self-imposed obligation rather than a mood. The gathering is then stated as certain, and the loss named is of oneself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah the commentators report as revealed as one unit late in the Meccan period, addressed to people who acknowledged a creator but attached others to Him. The argument runs by question and answer throughout, and this is its first instance. The community at that stage was small, pressured, and had no prospect of relief, which is the setting in which mercy is called an obligation God took on.

keyTerms.note: The verb for setting something down in writing, used of contracts and decrees. Applied to God and mercy, it makes the mercy binding by His own act, which the commentators stress was imposed by nobody else.
From a root connected with the womb. The word carries the sense of a protection that surrounds and sustains something helpless, which is why it is chosen here rather than a word for leniency.

keyTerms.gloss: they lost, they came out short
keyTerms.note: Commercial vocabulary for a trade that ended below where it started. The object of the loss is the traders themselves, so the ayah describes people who left the transaction short of a self.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on written and witnessed obligations. Trading partnerships, loans and the terms of a caravan's profit share were recorded and deposited, and a document hung inside the sanctuary carried its weight behind it. Men bound themselves in writing precisely because memory and honour were not enough. The verb used here of God's mercy was legal vocabulary before it was ever devotional.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that God has written mercy upon Himself appears twice in this surah and nowhere else in the Quran, here and again at 6:54. Both times it sits inside an instruction to say something aloud, so the sentence arrives as a message being delivered rather than as a description offered from outside.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ownership and obligation are usually opposites: whoever owns a thing owes nothing about how they use it. The ayah puts them in consecutive clauses and lets the second qualify the first, so absolute possession is immediately narrowed by a commitment nobody imposed. That gives a reader something firmer than hope in a temperament. And mercy precedes the gathering in the sentence, which the commentators do not treat as accidental.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same sentence about written mercy, applying it to those who repent.
States the scope of that mercy, saying it encompasses all things.
Draws the practical conclusion, telling those who despair not to.

studies.applyIt: If you carry a private suspicion that you have used up your allowance of second chances, notice where that idea actually comes from. It is not from here. This ayah puts mercy under a written commitment rather than under a mood, and a commitment does not change according to how recently you last tested it.

studies.title: None Can Lift It But He
studies.meaning: The messenger is told to say that he himself is afraid, which places him inside the same accountability as his listeners rather than above it. Two statements about agency follow. Being spared on that Day is called mercy, not achievement. And in the present, harm and good are each described as a touch from God, with the removal of harm reserved to Him alone, while the good needs no such clause because His power is stated as unrestricted.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah addressed to people pressing the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to soften or trade away the message. The ayat just before record their demands, and this is the answer: refusal is not stubbornness but fear of a specific consequence. The commentators read the closing ayah as widening the reply, since the people making the demands also believed themselves able to help or harm him.

keyTerms.note: The lightest verb available for contact, used of a hand brushing against something. Choosing it for both harm and good makes each minimal from the sender's side, whatever they feel like from ours.
From a root for lifting a cover off. Harm is pictured as something laid over a person rather than injected into them, so removing it means taking the covering away again.
A word for coming through successfully, used of escaping danger as much as of gaining a prize. It suits an ayah where the victory described consists of being turned away from something.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Illness, drought and loss were addressed in Arabia through intermediaries: charms tied to a child's arm, offerings left at a tribal shrine, a diviner consulted about who had caused a misfortune. Every affliction had a practical channel of appeal. The claim that harm can only be lifted by the one who allowed it removed the entire apparatus people reached for when something went wrong.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah repeatedly puts words into the Prophet's mouth with the command to say, and the instruction occurs dozens of times across its length, more often than in almost any other surah. Here the first thing he is told to say is that he is afraid, which is an unusual opening for someone arguing that he is right.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage relocates safety. If harm and its removal both come from one source, then negotiating with anyone else is not merely wrong but pointless, and fear is left with a single legitimate object. The reasoning is practical rather than abstract in tone. And by having the messenger declare his own fear first, the argument avoids the shape it would otherwise take, of a man warning others about a danger he considers himself exempt from.

crossReferences.why: States the same point about harm and bounty with different verbs, later in the Quran.
Asks whether the things called on beside God could remove a harm He intended.
Belongs to the same argument, answering who owns the heavens and the earth.

studies.applyIt: Next time something goes wrong and you start listing who to call, add one line at the start of the list rather than at the end. Ask for the thing directly, in your own words, before you begin the practical work. The ayah does not say the calls are useless. It says where the list actually begins.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: It Is Not You They Deny
studies.meaning: Two ayat that look unrelated and are not. The first calls the present life play and diversion, terms for activity that absorbs a person without producing anything, and ends with a question about using the mind. The second addresses a particular grief. The commentators follow the wording closely: the deniers are not calling the messenger a liar in their own estimation, they are rejecting the signs, and the ayah separates the man from what he carries.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage belongs to a stretch in which opponents mocked the message publicly while, according to reports the commentators preserve, privately conceding that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had never been known to lie. That gap is what the second ayah addresses. The surah as a whole belongs to a period of sustained argument and rejection rather than of physical persecution.

keyTerms.note: Activity with no result beyond itself, the word used of children's games. It is not condemned as evil, only as unproductive, which is why the ayah follows it with a question about using your mind.
What pulls attention away from something more important. The word's force is comparative: it names not the thing itself but its effect of turning a person from what they had meant to attend to.
A verb for rejecting what one recognises to be true, distinct from simply not believing. Its use here is why the commentators read the ayah as separating public denial from private assessment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan society ran on reputation, and a man's word was his commercial standing. Accusing someone of lying was a serious charge with consequences for his trade and his family, which is part of why opponents preferred to attack the message rather than the messenger's character. The Prophet had carried a byname for trustworthiness before any of this began, and that made him awkward to dismiss.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase calling this life play and diversion appears several times in the Quran, and in one place, at 57:20, it is expanded into a list of five stages that reads like a whole life in miniature: play, distraction, display, boasting, and competing in wealth and children. The short form here leaves that expansion to the reader.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Consolation is offered by correcting a fact rather than by softening one. The grief is acknowledged as real and then given a different object: what is being refused is not the person delivering it. That is a particular kind of comfort, available to anyone whose message is rejected, and it rests on a claim about where the message came from. The first ayah supplies the scale on which the whole exchange should be measured.

crossReferences.why: Expands the same description of worldly life into five stages ending in ruin or forgiveness.
Tells the Prophet not to let his soul waste away in grief over them.
Describes the same grief in stronger terms, almost destroying himself over their refusal.

studies.applyIt: Think of one criticism that has stayed with you longer than it deserved. Ask what was actually being rejected: the work, the idea, or you. Write the answer in a few words. Most of the sting in criticism comes from a merger this ayah takes apart, and separating them again is usually a matter of one sentence.

studies.title: Communities Like Your Own
studies.meaning: Every creature that walks and every bird that flies is called a community, using the same word the Quran uses of human nations. The comparison is stated plainly and then left standing, and the commentators differ over how far it reaches: some read it of their being ordered and provided for as we are, others of their having their own forms of accountability. A claim about the record follows, and then a gathering that includes them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside a passage arguing with people who wanted a sign delivered on demand. The ayah answers by pointing at signs already present in enormous number. The surah belongs to the later Meccan years, when the exchange had settled into a pattern of demands and refusals, and much of its method is to redirect attention from the spectacular towards what is already in view.

keyTerms.note: From a verb for moving slowly along the ground. The word covers every walking animal and is used elsewhere of human beings too, so the category the ayah opens with already includes the listener.
The same word used of human peoples with their own messengers and appointed terms. Applying it to animals is the ayah's whole claim, and Arabic offers no gentler reading of the word.
The verb used of people driven together at the resurrection, taken from the herding of livestock and the mustering of armies. Here it is applied to the animals themselves rather than to their owners.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs lived closer to animals than to most people. A herder knew individual camels by temperament, tracked birds to find water, and read the movement of gazelles for weather. Poetry of the period describes ostriches and wild asses with a precision that only comes from watching them for hours. An audience like that would not have found animal societies a strange idea; they had watched the orders and hierarchies.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the bird flying with its two wings has drawn comment since the earliest period, because flight already implies wings. Classical commentators read the redundancy as a way of pinning the description to something actually seen rather than to birds as a category, holding the sentence to what is concrete.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah decentres the human being without demoting them. Other creatures are given the vocabulary of community and of gathering, which places them inside the moral architecture of the world rather than beside it as furniture. The middle clause makes a further claim, that nothing has been left out of the record, and the commentators differ over whether that record means this revelation or the preserved book of all things.

crossReferences.why: Says that birds in flight and all in the heavens each know their own prayer.
States that everything glorifies God, though people do not understand their praise.
Places the provision of every moving creature on God, in a nearby surah.

studies.applyIt: Watch one animal today for two full minutes: a bird on a wire, a cat crossing a wall, ants at a crack in the pavement. Do not photograph it. The ayah calls what you are looking at a community, and the claim only becomes interesting once you have watched long enough to notice that something is being organised.

studies.title: Say Peace To Them
studies.meaning: The instruction is about a greeting. When believers come, the first words are peace, before anything is taught or corrected. What follows is given as the content of that greeting: mercy is a written commitment, and the conditions attached are unusually gentle. Wrongdoing done in ignorance, then turning back, then repair. The commentators read ignorance broadly, covering anyone who acted without weighing what they were doing, which is most people much of the time.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayat just before describe pressure on the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to send away the poor followers who had nothing to offer, so that the leading men of Mecca could listen without losing face. The refusal of that demand is what this passage follows. The greeting instructed here is addressed to exactly the people he was being asked to dismiss.

keyTerms.note: From a root for wholeness and being free of defect. As a greeting it declares that no harm is intended, and it is the word the Quran uses of the greeting exchanged in the Garden.
Not a lack of information. Commentators explain it as acting without regard for consequence, the state of a person who knew and did not weigh it, which is why the term covers so much ground.

A verb for repairing what has broken, used of mending relations between people. It adds a third step after regret and turning back, and it points outward at the damage rather than inward at the feeling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Greetings in Arabia were social placement. Who you greeted first, whether you greeted at all, and which formula you used declared rank in public. A man of standing was greeted before he greeted, and being passed over was a recognised humiliation. Instructing the Prophet to open with peace towards followers of no consequence inverted a rule everybody watching would have noticed at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about mercy being written appears twice in this surah, and the difference between the two is instructive. At 6:12 it stands inside an argument with opponents about who owns the world. Here it is placed inside a greeting to believers, so the same sentence works once as evidence and once as reassurance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness is described in three moves rather than one: the act, the turning, and the repair. That refuses a version of repentance which is entirely interior. The passage also puts the offer inside a greeting, which changes its register; it is not a warning with a concession attached but news delivered to people already in the room. And the ayah after says that clarity itself exposes the other path.

crossReferences.why: Names the same condition, wrongdoing done in ignorance followed by turning back soon after.
Shows the angels greeting the patient with peace, the same word used here.
Refuses the demand to drive away those who call on their Lord morning and evening.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone comes to you with something they have done wrong, notice what your first sentence is. Try making it an ordinary greeting, the kind you would give anyone, before you say anything about the matter. The order in this ayah is deliberate, and it puts the person in the room before the problem.

studies.title: The Keys Of The Unseen
studies.meaning: The image is of keys, held by one holder, to what nobody else can open. Then the description narrows instead of expanding, which is the ayah's method: from land and sea, to a single falling leaf, to a seed underground in the dark, to whatever is moist or dry. The commentators note the movement from the vast to the negligible. What ends the sentence is not knowledge but a record, so nothing observed is left unwritten.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah largely occupied with people who wanted proof and with the limits of what human beings can establish for themselves. The ayat around it describe God taking souls at night and returning them by day. The commentators record no occasion for this one, and read it as part of the surah's sustained argument about the difference between what people know and what they assume.

keyTerms.note: The plural can be read as keys or as treasuries, and the classical commentators record both. Either way the point is access: what stands behind them cannot be reached without the one who holds them.
What is absent from perception, not what is mysterious in itself. The word is relative to the observer, which is why the ayah has to add that only He knows these particular things.
The singular form with its feminine ending names one individual leaf rather than foliage in general. That grammatical choice is what makes the example small enough to do the work the sentence needs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: For farmers and herders the buried seed was the standing image of uncertainty. You put grain into dark ground and waited months with no way of knowing what had happened to it, and a season's food hung on that hidden interval. The ayah names exactly that, along with the wet and the dry, the two words a desert people used to divide everything that grows.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah is one of a small group in the Quran built entirely as a descending list, moving from the widest category to the smallest without a break. It contains no command and no address to the listener, and it is among the passages classical commentators return to when discussing what is meant by the clear record named at its end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Divine knowledge is described through the trivial rather than the impressive, which is the harder claim to make. Knowing the count of the stars would be a lesser statement than knowing about one leaf, because the leaf falls beneath the threshold at which anything would normally be recorded. That lands in two directions at once: nothing a person suffers is beneath notice, and nothing done quietly goes unregistered either.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the claim about the smallest weight, in earth or heaven, being in a clear record.
Lists specific things kept with God alone, naming keys this ayah leaves unopened.
Insists that no atom's weight escapes Him, answering those who deny the Hour.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have been doing that nobody has noticed: a repeated kindness, a restraint no one sees, a difficulty you have not mentioned. Let this ayah be about that rather than about the universe for a moment. It is built out of the smallest examples available, and that appears to be the point of it.

studies.title: His Word Is The Truth
studies.meaning: Creation is said to be in truth, meaning with a purpose rather than as a game, and that phrase governs everything after it. Then the mode of creation: a word said, and the thing is. The commentators note the tense, since the sentence describes a day still ahead while using a present verb, which keeps one act of command over both the first creation and the raising. Sovereignty is then named specifically for the day the trumpet sounds.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a passage that has followed Abraham's argument with his people and then run through a list of prophets. The surah addresses an audience who accepted God as creator while treating other powers as intermediaries, and this ayah answers by leaving no room for a second authority on the day it would matter most. The commentators report no particular occasion for it.

keyTerms.note: The word covers truth, right and what is due. Saying the heavens were made with it denies that creation is arbitrary, and the same word returns two clauses later to describe God's own speech.
The bare imperative of the verb to be, two letters in Arabic. It is the shortest command the language can form, and the shortness is the point: nothing stands between the intention and the thing.
A curved horn of the kind used to summon people or signal an army. The Quran uses it for the blast that ends and then restarts everything, and here it fixes the moment sovereignty becomes undeniable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Authority in Mecca was distributed among clans by office and by custom, and nobody held all of it. Decisions were taken in assembly, alliances shifted, and the man who seemed dominant one season could be outmanoeuvred the next. A claim that sovereignty on a particular day belongs to one holder alone, with no assembly and no negotiating, described something nobody present had ever experienced.
studies.didYouKnow: The command translated as be is a single word of two letters in Arabic, and it occurs several times in the Quran, always in the same construction. In each case the response is given in the same breath, with no gap between command and result, so the grammar itself refuses any interval in which the thing might not yet exist.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Creation and resurrection are collapsed into one kind of act. If the first required nothing but a word, the second cannot be harder, and that is the argument the ayah makes without stating it. Naming God as knower of both the hidden and the witnessed then closes a gap a listener might use: no domain, private or public, is held back from the same authority. The closing names concern wisdom and detail rather than force.

crossReferences.why: States the same command and its instant answer, arguing directly for the resurrection.
Applies the same phrasing to the origination of the heavens and the earth.
Describes the two blasts of the trumpet and what happens between them.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you keep postponing because the first step feels heavy. Do the smallest possible version of it within the next hour, not the whole thing. This ayah puts no distance between a word and its effect, and while nothing human works that way, most of the distance we experience turns out to be added by us.

studies.title: When The Sun Went Down
studies.meaning: The sequence ends here. Abraham has watched a star, then the moon, then the sun, each time calling it his lord and then withdrawing when it set. The commentators differ over whether he was reasoning his own way towards God or arguing with his people by adopting their premise and following it to collapse. Either way the conclusion is not that the sun is small, but that whatever sets cannot be what he is looking for.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is largely an argument with people who worshipped God alongside other powers, and Abraham is introduced as the ancestor they claimed. The commentators note the strategic point: the figure Mecca traced its lineage and its sanctuary back to is shown rejecting exactly the arrangement his descendants had settled into. No specific occasion is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: A word for something bursting into view, used of dawn and of blood from a wound. It gives the sun's appearance a suddenness that makes its later setting all the more pointed.
A legal term for being clear of a liability or a charge. Using it here makes the break formal rather than emotional, the way a man publicly renounces a debt he will not carry.
One who turns from the surrounding practice towards what is upright. The Quran uses it repeatedly of Abraham, and it describes a direction taken rather than a doctrine held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Astral religion was familiar across Arabia and its neighbours. Particular tribes were associated with particular heavenly bodies, and caravans navigated by the same stars they invoked. Anyone travelling at night knew the order of risings and settings intimately. Abraham's argument works because his audience were expert observers: they knew better than anyone that everything in that sky goes down.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage is one of very few places in the Quran that stages a line of reasoning step by step, with the conclusion reached at the end rather than announced at the start. The classical commentators disagree about whether it records Abraham's own search or a technique of debate, and both readings have been held by major authorities.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test applied is disappearance. Whatever cannot stay is disqualified, and that criterion is available to anyone with patience and a horizon, requiring no text and no teacher. The passage also models a public break with inherited practice, which is costly in any society organised by lineage. The declaration at the end is about direction, a face turned, rather than about assent to a proposition.

crossReferences.why: Gives the earlier steps of the same sequence, the star and then the moon.
Tells the other Abraham story, the broken idols and the question put to his people.
Shows him arguing about a lord who gives life, with the sun brought into it again.

studies.applyIt: Take something you rely on for a sense of stability: a job, one person's approval, a number in an account. Ask what happens to your footing if it goes, and answer honestly rather than bravely. Abraham's test was not contempt for what he was watching. It was noticing what those things do at the end of the day.

studies.title: Which Side Deserves Security
studies.meaning: The argument is turned around. Abraham is being threatened with the anger of the gods, and he answers by asking who should be afraid of whom, given that his opponents attached partners to God with no warrant sent down for it. The question about which party has more right to safety is left for them to answer. The ayah after supplies it, and the condition attached, faith not clouded by wrongdoing, is what the commentators discuss most.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing Abraham's dispute with his people directly after his renunciation of what they worshipped. The surrounding surah applies the exchange to its own audience, who had warned the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that their deities might strike him. Classical sources preserve reports of early listeners troubled by the second ayah, who took the word for wrongdoing in its widest sense.

keyTerms.note: A word for a sanction or proof that gives someone the right to act, and later for a ruler. Its use here demands documentation: the practice is challenged for having nothing issued behind it.
From the same root as faith and trust. The word for being safe and the word for believing come from one source, which is why the ayah can move between them without changing subject.
A verb for clothing something or covering it over, used of confusing truth with falsehood. Faith is pictured as a garment that can be worn with something else layered on top of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear of offending a tribal deity was practical rather than theoretical. Shrines were credited with causing illness, drought or a failed journey when slighted, and people arranged their travel and their oaths accordingly. Threatening someone with a god's displeasure was a real threat in that world. Abraham's reply does not deny that fear is reasonable; it asks which of the two positions is actually exposed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for security shares its root with the word for faith, and the two stand in the same sentence at the close of the passage. Arabic lets the ayah make its point through sound as well as sense, since a listener hears the connection between believing and being safe before the argument has been spelled out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Safety is presented as a consequence of what is true rather than of what is powerful. The question about which party has more right to it assumes that security follows accuracy, and that a person aligned with reality stands differently from one who is not, regardless of who is currently frightened. The qualifying clause then keeps that from turning complacent, since faith is described as something that can be clouded over.

crossReferences.why: Names associating partners with God as a great wrong, the reading given to this passage.
Precedes the argument, where his people dispute with him and he refuses to fear.
Describes God as the ally of believers, bringing them out of darkness into light.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are quietly afraid of that has been shaping your decisions this month. Then ask Abraham's question about it: what is it actually able to do, and on what authority. You are not talking yourself out of the fear. You are checking whether it has the standing you have been giving it.

studies.title: No Vision Can Grasp Him
studies.meaning: The first ayah gathers a long argument into a conclusion, naming God as Lord and creator of everything and drawing worship as the consequence. The second states a limit. Sight does not reach Him while He reaches sight, and the commentators record a long discussion of what exactly that rules out. The two divine names closing it are unexpected: not power or majesty, but subtlety and expert awareness, words about closeness rather than distance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a passage that has argued against attributing offspring and partners to God. The surah addresses people who acknowledged a creator and then hedged that acknowledgement with intermediaries they could see and handle. The ayah about vision speaks directly into that, and the commentators read the pairing as answering a demand for something visible to worship rather than as an abstract statement.

keyTerms.note: The term for an agent entrusted with another's affairs. Applied to God over all things, it makes maintenance rather than mere origination the point: the world is not left running on its own.
A verb for catching up with something and encompassing it, used of a pursuer reaching what he chases. What is denied is comprehension by sight, which is where the classical discussion begins.
From a root for fineness and delicacy. It carries both being too fine to be perceived and being gentle in dealing with small things, and the commentators keep both senses active here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Worship in Mecca was tactile. Idols were washed, dressed, touched for blessing and carried on journeys, and the sanctuary held images a pilgrim could stand in front of. Religion was something done with the hands and the eyes. Telling that audience their sight could not reach the one they should worship removed the ordinary equipment of devotion and left only words and conduct.
studies.didYouKnow: The two names that close the second ayah appear together several times in the Quran, and almost always in contexts about hidden things: a grain inside a rock, a deed nobody saw, a private grief. The pairing joins fineness of perception to gentleness of treatment, which is why translators struggle to render the first with any single English word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage guards worship against its likeliest failure, which is not disbelief but reduction. If the object of worship could be grasped by sight, it would be an object among others and could be handled accordingly. Denying that while affirming that He grasps all vision reverses the usual relation between the seer and the seen. The closing names then keep the inaccessibility from reading as remoteness.

crossReferences.why: States that nothing is like Him, closing with names about hearing and seeing.
Records Moses asking to see, and what happened to the mountain instead.
Uses the same name for subtle awareness, asking whether the creator would not know.

studies.applyIt: Notice the picture that appears in your mind when you pray, whatever it is: a direction, a light, a presence somewhere above. Do not try to correct it into nothing. Just let it be inadequate rather than accurate, and carry on. The ayah is not asking you to stop imagining; it is telling you what your imagining is not.

studies.title: Come, I Will Recite It
studies.meaning: A public invitation opens the list, and the phrasing is careful: what follows is what your Lord has made unlawful, recited rather than argued. The items alternate between prohibitions and one positive command about parents, which sits inside the series rather than beside it. Killing children out of poverty is answered mid-sentence with a statement about provision. The commentators note that indecency is named in both its open and its concealed forms.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the end of a surah that has spent its length disputing with people over what they had declared off limits on their own authority. The immediately preceding ayat challenge those self-made prohibitions. This passage answers them by reciting what was actually enjoined, and the commentators treat the sequence as deliberate: a false list is set aside and a true one read out in its place.

keyTerms.note: An imperative meaning to come towards a higher place, used to call someone over. It opens the passage as an invitation rather than a summons, and it is addressed to opponents in the middle of a dispute.
Not general hardship but the condition of having nothing left at all. The word names the actual pressure behind the practice being addressed, which the ayah answers by naming who provides.
The plural of a word for what is excessive and shameful. The ayah divides it into what appears and what is concealed, so the category is defined by the act rather than by whether anyone saw it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Infant burial in times of famine is attested in the poetry and the reports of pre-Islamic Arabia, driven by the arithmetic of a bad season: mouths that could not be fed in a household with no reserve. The Quran addresses the practice more than once, and each time it attaches a statement about provision to the prohibition, answering the calculation rather than only the act.
studies.didYouKnow: This passage and the two ayat after it have been read since early times as a parallel to the commandments given to Moses, and classical commentators note the resemblance directly. The list here begins where those do, with associating nothing with God and honouring parents, and it closes with a call to understand rather than with a threat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The list is introduced as recitation, which places its authority outside the speaker, and that is the whole point of the surah's argument: the difference between what God has enjoined and what a community has decided among itself. Placing kindness to parents inside a series of prohibitions has been read as showing that some obligations cannot be met by abstention alone. The stated purpose at the end is understanding.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the prohibition on killing children from fear of poverty, reversing the order of provision.
Continues the same recitation through weights, speech, and the straight path.
Lists what has actually been forbidden, open indecency and hidden alike.

studies.applyIt: The ayah divides wrongdoing into what shows and what does not. Pick the quietest item on your own list, the thing nobody would ever hear about, and do one concrete thing this week that makes continuing it harder. Not a resolution, an arrangement. The hidden half is the half that survives on being unmentioned.

studies.title: Ten For One
studies.meaning: The rate of exchange is stated plainly, and it is not equal. A good deed brought is answered tenfold; a bad one is answered with its like and no more. The commentators attend to the wording of both halves: the good is multiplied, and elsewhere in the Quran the ceiling is left open, while the bad is capped by a word for equivalence. The closing clause explains why the asymmetry is not unfairness, since nobody receives less than they earned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of a surah largely occupied with argument and warning. Its final ayat turn from dispute to a statement of terms, and this is one of them. The commentators record no occasion for it and read the placement as deliberate: after a long confrontation about what people had invented, the surah closes by setting out plainly how the account is actually kept.

keyTerms.note: The verb for arriving carrying something, rather than for doing it. It pictures the deed as an item brought to a counter, which is why the response is described as a rate rather than as a verdict.

The multiplier is stated as ten likenesses of the thing itself, not ten of something else. What is returned keeps the shape of what was given, magnified rather than exchanged for a different currency.

The passive of the verb for putting something out of its place. Its use here defines fairness as receiving no less than what is due, which leaves the extra given to a good deed outside the calculation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan trade ran on rates of exchange, and everyone present understood a multiplier. A merchant financed a caravan expecting a return several times the outlay, and profit was reckoned in shares agreed before departure. Putting the moral account in that language used terms the audience handled daily, and the tenfold figure would have been heard as a rate of return rather than as a metaphor.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere raises the multiplier well beyond ten: one passage compares a good deed to a grain producing seven ears with a hundred grains in each, and adds that God multiplies further for whom He wills. The figure of ten here is therefore the floor of what is promised rather than its limit, and the commentators read the two together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The asymmetry is the doctrine. If mercy is written into the accounting itself, then hope is not a mood a person has to work up but a fact about the ledger. Capping the penalty at equivalence keeps justice intact, so the generosity costs nothing in fairness. Between them the two halves describe a system tilted in one direction on purpose, and the tilt is stated as policy rather than as a favour.

crossReferences.why: Raises the same multiplication far higher with the image of a grain and seven ears.
States that God does not wrong by an atom's weight and doubles a good deed.
Repeats the same asymmetry in a Meccan surah, with better than the deed for the good.

studies.applyIt: Do one small good thing today that you would normally skip because it seems too minor to count: a message of thanks, a plate washed that is not yours. The whole argument of this ayah is about scale, and it says the scale is not yours to judge. Your part is only the bringing.

studies.title: My Living And My Dying
studies.meaning: Four things are named and handed over in a single clause: prayer, offering, life and death. The first two are acts of worship; the second two are not acts at all, which is what makes the list unusual. The commentators read it as extending devotion past what a person does into what merely happens to them. The declaration then closes with a claim about being first, which they explain as first among this community rather than in history.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, the closing declaration of a surah that has argued at length with people who dedicated animals and crops to various powers. The instruction to say this is therefore pointed: the practices disputed throughout the surah are exactly the ones being reassigned here. The commentators read these ayat as the surah's summation, delivered in the first person rather than as one more argument.

keyTerms.note: A word for the animal offered and for acts of devotion generally. Its root also carries washing and purity, so the term joins a physical offering to the idea of being made clean.
A noun for the whole of a life rather than for the act of living. Paired with its counterpart it covers the span a person does not control, placing that under the same dedication as their prayer.

The commentators explain first as foremost within this community rather than earliest in time, since the Quran describes earlier prophets in the same terms. It marks priority of commitment, not chronology.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Animals were dedicated by name in pre-Islamic Arabia. A camel might be marked for a particular deity, its ear slit, its milk reserved, and a slaughter was announced with the name of the power it was offered to. Everyone present heard whose it was. In that setting, declaring the recipient of an offering was a public act of allegiance rather than a private intention.
studies.didYouKnow: These two ayat are among the passages many Muslims recite inside the prayer itself, in the opening supplication reported in the classical collections. A statement that begins with the word prayer therefore ends up being spoken during one, a circularity the commentators note when discussing where the passage came to be used.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sincerity is defined by scope rather than by intensity. The list moves from the deliberate to the involuntary, so what is offered includes the parts of a life a person did not choose and cannot perform. That makes the declaration impossible to complete by effort, which is the point of it: a statement of ownership rather than a report of achievement. The denial of any partner then restates the same sentence.

crossReferences.why: Describes sincere devotion as the whole of what was ever commanded.
Uses the same language of turning one's face over to God while doing good.
States that the flesh of offerings does not reach God, only the awareness behind them.

studies.applyIt: Before something ordinary today, a meal, a commute, opening your laptop, say quietly who it is for. Not a long formula. These ayat put living and dying in the same list as prayer, which suggests the offering is meant to cover the unremarkable hours, and those are the ones nobody thinks to dedicate.
